title: Deterministic \(2^{n-\Omega(n/k)}\)-time counting for \(k\)-SAT
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c\in(0,1)\) such that for every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), some deterministic algorithm \(A_k\) exactly counts the satisfying assignments of every \(k\)-CNF formula on \(n\) variables within time \[ C_k\,2^{\,n-cn/k}(N+2)^{b_k}, \] for constants \(C_k\ge1\) and integers \(b_k\ge1\), where \(N\) is the input’s bit length and the computation uses the bit-cost random-access model below? The constants and program may depend on \(k\); the constant \(c\) may not.
why: The question asks whether deterministic exact counting can retain an exponential saving comparable to that for satisfiability when clause width is fixed. It isolates the cost of removing randomness from a canonical counting problem while tracking how the saving deteriorates as the fixed width increases.
status_note: Resolved by Chan and Williams, preliminary SODA 2016 and ACM Transactions on Algorithms 17(1), Article 2 (2021 issue), Theorem 1.6. The author manuscript explicitly names the 2013 Santhanam problem and its proof supplies the reciprocal-width saving for every fixed k. The original statement, theorem and proof were read, and publication metadata was checked in the University of Illinois record. The ACM landing page returned HTTP 403; it is not claimed as read. This is a literature-resolution audit, not a Lean-verified submission or an optimal-exponent theorem.

sentences: The task is to count all satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula whose clauses have a fixed maximum width.
The 2013 question asks for deterministic time with an exponential saving proportional to the number of variables divided by that width.
The saving must use one positive absolute constant across all fixed widths, while polynomial factors may depend on the width.
Chan and Williams proved the required exact-counting bound and explicitly identified the original question as resolved.
The historical open card is retired with its statement and provenance preserved, separately from questions about the optimal counting exponent.

definitions:
The variables are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), for \(n\ge1\). A literal is either \(x_i\) or its negation. A clause is a disjunction of at most \(k\) literals, and a \(k\)-CNF formula is a conjunction of finitely many such clauses. Repeated clauses, repeated literals and unused variables are allowed. An empty clause is false; an empty conjunction is true. The desired output is the integer \[ \#F=|\{a\in\{0,1\}^n:F(a)=1\}| \] in binary, including the contribution of all declared variables, not just those that occur.

The input gives \(n\) in unary and an explicit clause list with delimiters and binary variable indices and signs. Its full length is \(N\). For each fixed \(k\), the program \(A_k\) receives arbitrary such inputs; no restriction on the number of supplied clauses is imposed. Reading, validating or simplifying the formula and writing the answer are included in the running time. The parameter \(k\) is fixed before \(n\) varies, rather than being a growing-width parameter with one prescribed polynomial overhead.

Use a deterministic bit-cost random-access machine with a fixed finite program, integer registers and memory cells indexed by nonnegative integers. The input is a read-only bit array and auxiliary storage initially contains zero. Allowed operations are copying, indexed reads and writes, comparisons and branches, Boolean bit operations and shifts on nonnegative integers, and exact integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor. Signed integers use a sign and binary magnitude. There is no unit-cost real arithmetic, exponentiation instruction, oracle, random instruction, advice or precomputed input-dependent data. An elementary operation is charged \((1+\ell)^2\) units, where \(\ell\) is the sum of the bit lengths of all integer operands, results and accessed addresses in that operation; a control operation with no operands costs one. Multiword and table computations pay for their constituent operations. This conservative bit-cost convention allows exponential address ranges while charging for their descriptions. Polynomial bit overhead is included in the displayed factor \((N+2)^{b_k}\).

The guarantee is worst-case and exact on every valid formula. Formally the quantifier order is \(\exists c\ \forall k\ge3\ \exists A_k,C_k,b_k\ \forall n,F\). No uniform bound in \(k\) on the program size, preprocessing constant, or exponent \(b_k\) is imposed, and no map constructing \(A_k\) from \(k\) is separately required. This is the source’s fixed-clause-width exponential-rate question. The saving coefficient \(c/k\) must use a single positive \(c\) across all fixed widths.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the algorithm family and bounds with one absolute \(c>0\), or prove the logical negation. Correctness requires the exact number of satisfying assignments, not merely existence of an assignment, approximate counting, or parity of the count. The source asks an algorithm-existence question; it is not a request for the numerical value of \(\#F\) on one instance. A randomized algorithm or a saving only of order \(n/2^k\) does not establish the target.

context_blocks.text: Santhanam’s 2013 question specifically asks for a deterministic \(\#k\)-SAT algorithm running in \(2^{n-\Omega(n/k)}\) time. It is not a request to determine an arbitrary optimal exponent curve. The accompanying remark credits a randomized counting algorithm with that rate. The source’s separate comment about a particular decision-SAT rate is not the main target of this card.

The fixed-width convention matters. A bound \(2^{n-n/O(2^k)}\) gives a positive saving for each fixed \(k\), but the saving becomes much smaller as \(k\) increases than the requested \(1/O(k)\) fraction of the exponent. Polynomial input-size factors are allowed; they do not change these exponential rates for fixed \(k\) after redundant clauses are removed.

Chan and Williams’s Theorem 1.6 gives deterministic exact counting in \(2^{n-n/O(k)}\) time for every constant \(k\). The theorem explicitly identifies Santhanam’s question as resolved. Its proof chooses an absolute constant in the reciprocal-width saving and suppresses polynomial factors; it computes the count rather than deciding satisfiability.

The author manuscript retains placeholder journal metadata, so publication details were checked in the institutional record. The result appeared in preliminary form at SODA 2016 and in the January 2021 journal issue. The historical open record is retired without claiming that the optimal deterministic counting exponent is known or that a Lean solution has been submitted.
